paragraphs: Yochanan the High Priest.

His grandfather was Matityahu son of Yochanan son of Shimon, of the descendants of Yehoyariv in Jerusalem, who lived on Mount Modi'it. God blessed him with five sons: Yochanan, Shimon, Yehudah the Maccabee, Eleazar and Yonatan. Through them God brought deliverance to His people Israel, and they made an everlasting name that would not be cut off. All four of his sons fell in battle after fighting the Lord’s war for several years; the last of them was Shimon. In his days the land of Judea rested from war, and he did only good for his people. He concluded a treaty of peace with the kingdom of Rome. For all the benefits he had conferred on his people Israel, they began writing in their chronicles and all their documents, “In the first year of Shimon the High Priest, ruler and prince of the Jews.” Shimon the High Priest had three sons, named Yehudah, Matityahu and Yochanan (Hyrcanus), and one daughter, who married Ptolemy son of Abubus, an official in the plains of Jericho and a very wealthy man. But he was an evil, worthless man of the Sadducean party. By a trick he brought his father-in-law Shimon and Shimon’s sons Yehudah and Matityahu to a feast he held in the fortress “Dakh,” in the vicinity of Jericho, and there he killed them. He also wished to capture Shimon’s son Yochanan. But when Yochanan learned of it, he hurried to the gates of Jerusalem and seized the kingship. This is related in the Books of the Hasmoneans. It is about this Yochanan the High Priest that Abaye and Rava disagree in Berakhot 29. Abaye says, “Yannai and Yochanan are one and the same”; Rava says, “Yannai is one person and Yochanan another: Yannai was wicked from the outset, whereas Yochanan was righteous from the outset.” And this is indeed the truth, for Yochanan the High Priest was righteous for most of his life and practiced justice and charity. So great was he in the eyes of his people that, as related in Rosh Hashanah 18b, they instituted the wording in legal documents, “In such-and-such a year of Yochanan, High Priest of God Most High.”[^1]

We have already explained several times the view of the eminent author of Dorot HaRishonim: there were almost always two high priests. One was the high priest who served as the nation’s prince in place of a king; the other was the high priest who performed the high-priestly service in the Temple. This was because the high-priestly princes were generally occupied with war and were often away from Jerusalem. With Yochanan the High Priest, however, we find that he himself performed the service on Yom Kippur, as expressly stated in Sotah 33a. (He had sent his two sons Antigonus and Aristobulus to fight the Samaritans and destroy their temple on Mount Gerizim.) While he was in the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, he heard a heavenly voice saying, “The young men who went to wage war at Antioch have been victorious.” They noted the time, and it corresponded to the very hour of the victory. (So it is in the Tosefta there, chapter 13.)

Of him they said in Yoma 9a that he served as high priest for eighty years. It is very difficult to understand their holy words: they said that during the Second Temple’s four hundred and twenty years, more than three hundred priests served in it—“subtract from them the forty years in which Shimon the Righteous served, and the eighty of Yochanan the High Priest,” etc. Did they not know that Yonatan and Shimon, the brothers of Yehudah the Maccabee, also served as high priests, as did King Yannai, who was high priest, and afterward his sons Hyrcanus and Aristobulus?

But this is strong evidence for what we have said: not all the high priests served in the Temple on Yom Kippur; rather, they displayed their high-priestly office only on the festival day during Sukkot. Thus, although Yochanan was high priest for only about thirty years, as expressly stated in Yosifin, when they said that he served as high priest for eighty years, the meaning is that the entire high priesthood of the Hasmoneans lasted about eighty years. This they had received as a trustworthy tradition. This is also the view of Massa Eretz Yisrael, page 20.[^2] In Parah 3:5 it says that Yochanan the High Priest prepared two red heifers; in Ma'aser Sheni 5:15 and Sotah 9:10, that he removed the tithe, abolished the “awakeners” and the “strikers,” that until his days the hammer struck in Jerusalem, and that in his days no one needed to inquire about demai. The Gemara in Sotah there explains all his enactments at length.[^3]

To understand their brief statement in Berakhot 29a—that Yochanan the High Priest served as high priest for eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee—we must ask: how could such a great elder, who throughout his life had followed the teaching of the Pharisees and been completely righteous, and upon whom the holy spirit sometimes rested, suddenly become utterly wicked, kill the sages of Israel, angrily persecute the sages of the Sanhedrin and establish a Sanhedrin of Sadducees? We must explain at some length the affairs of the Sadducees: how and when this sect arose in Israel. As the basis of our discussion, we shall take the true account written by the eminent scholar, the author of Dorot HaRishonim, in volume 1.

Many years before the persecutions under Antiochus, and before it had occurred to him to interfere in the Jews’ internal religious affairs, there were already some Israelites who wished to imitate the Greeks. They were powerful men who exercised great force. This party arose in the days of Yosef son of Toviah, the son of the sister of Chonyo son of Shimon the Righteous. He took control of the tax farming and stripped the skin from their bones; he, his sons and the entire company of tax collectors amassed very, very great wealth.

This in fact began, according to the tradition of our sages, in the days of Antigonus of Sokho. Two of his disciples were named Tzadok and Boethus, and from them arose the sects of the Sadducees and Boethusians. Over the course of decades they gained strength and took all the offices of government into their hands. Even when the land of Israel passed from the rule of the kings of Egypt to that of the kings of Syria, and the sale of the tax franchise was abolished, they had already become men of force who said, “The land is ours.” They pressed the kings of Syria to introduce the Greek religion into Judea, so that they would become a different people.

Their first act, when King Antiochus Epiphanes ascended the throne of Syria, was to buy and bribe him with their silver and gold to remove the upright Chonyo from the high priesthood. The wicked Jason took his place and corrupted his conduct on earth to a most appalling degree. But this dreadful party was not satisfied, for despite all his wickedness, Jason still did not dare to practice idolatry openly in the streets of Jerusalem. They therefore drove him out as well and appointed the utterly lawless “Menelaus” as high priest. Then began the days of terrible upheaval, as related at length in the Book of the Hasmoneans. Matityahu the priest and his valiant sons arose to save their people and their Torah, and through terrible wars over three consecutive years, those faithful to their religion succeeded in overcoming the Greeks.

All Matityahu’s sons died heroic deaths in the religious war. The first was Eleazar, the brother of Yehudah the Maccabee. After Yehudah’s wondrous victories, and after he had purified the Temple of the desolating abomination, the citadel nevertheless remained in the hands of Israel’s lawless men, who inflicted harm for many years. When Yehudah besieged the citadel to capture it, they sent messengers to King Eupator, the son of Antiochus, to save them. The king sent one hundred thousand infantry against Yehudah. In this great battle Eleazar, the brother of Yehudah the Maccabee, fell a heroic death. The general Lysias and his great army besieged the Temple for many days. Only through a miracle were they saved on this occasion, and the two sides made peace.

But the empty and reckless Hellenizers among Israel, with Eliakim the priest at their head, went to the king of Syria and cried out against Yehudah and his people. The king listened to them, invested Eliakim as high priest and sent the general Bacchides to wreak judgment upon Yehudah and his people. When Eliakim and Bacchides came to Jerusalem, all the sages of Israel went out to meet him and make peace, saying, “He is a priest and our brother, and he will not betray his brothers.” And so it was: he called to them in peace and swore that he would not harm them. But immediately he violated his oath and wrought great slaughter among them. At that time his uncle Yossi ben Yoezer was killed, as explained in his entry. Another dreadful calamity then befell Yehudah, for Eliakim fought for the high priesthood and shed much blood. Yehudah saw that Eliakim and his band of evildoers had done far worse than the gentiles; he strengthened himself in God and went out against them to battle once more. God wrought a great deliverance: the general Nicanor was killed, and the people’s spirits revived a little. But Eliakim and Bacchides did not despair. They came against Yehudah again, and this time Yehudah fell a heroic death. The lawless men, with Eliakim at their head, nearly raised their heads again. But Yonatan, Yehudah’s brother, was immediately anointed as leader. After many battles, they were defeated before the Israelites; Eliakim died an unnatural death, and when Bacchides saw that Eliakim was dead, he returned to his own land. The land rested for two years. The lawless men, however, again persuaded the king of Syria, who sent Bacchides to war once more. Yonatan and his brother Shimon struck him a great blow, and then they made peace. The Hasmoneans arose and cut off the transgressors from the land. Although this accursed party, deprived of its office, would neither rest nor be still, Yonatan’s hand was always raised above them. When the righteous Yonatan fell into Tryphon’s hands and was killed, his brother Shimon was immediately appointed leader. He fought the Lord’s war, and for nearly all Shimon’s days the land rested from war.

The transgressors and Hellenizers did not raise their heads throughout Shimon’s days, but hid in their holes, hoping to seize a favorable moment. They would neither rest nor be still until they had almost attained their heart’s desire. One of them was the wealthy Ptolemy, the son-in-law of Shimon the High Priest. He killed his father-in-law and two of his sons, sent agents to Jerusalem to kill Shimon’s son Yochanan as well, and wrote to the king of Syria to send him an army with which to take possession of Judea. From this we can understand that these crafty snakes were scattered everywhere. Ptolemy trusted that his friends in Jerusalem would quickly rise up. But Yochanan, who was then at Gezer, forestalled the disaster: he put the agents to death, captured Jerusalem and drove Ptolemy out. Yochanan the High Priest was indeed a righteous man who had been raised from his youth in the teaching of the Pharisees. His heart was whole with the Lord, God of Israel, and His Torah. He deviated neither to the right nor to the left from the Written Torah or the Oral Torah, nor from any of the rabbinic enactments: all were sacred in his eyes. He himself served as high priest and instituted enactments in Israel. The entire Sanhedrin consisted of holy men of the Most High. Its president was Yehoshua ben Perachya and its head of court Nittai the Arbelite. In his days they enjoyed abundant peace.

The transgressors and sinners who wished to assimilate among the Greeks, whose sole aim was to rule the people, suck out their substance, strip off their skin and fill their holes with gold, saw that disaster had overtaken them: the Greeks had withdrawn from the land and Israel’s right hand was raised high. They changed their approach a little. Instead of assimilating among the Greeks, they said, “What need have we of the Oral Torah and the rabbinic enactments?” They denied the resurrection of the dead and said there was only one world, and that we need only enjoy this world. Thus they brought forth a new generation: from the root of snakes came vipers. Since they had from earliest times been the powerful and wealthy men, and the wealthy have many friends, they would neither rest nor be still. In secret they plotted how to make peace with Yochanan the High Priest and gain a foothold in his palace.

Yochanan himself saw and understood that great danger threatened from this large party living among the people. He had continually to fear an enemy both within and without. He had seen with his own eyes that, had he delayed when his father was killed and not reached Jerusalem first, Ptolemy and his associates would have gained the upper hand. Although he had taken all their offices from them and they had dispersed among the people, the danger had not passed. Thus, although Yochanan was faithful to his God and His Torah, for the sake of the country’s peace he did not persecute them. On the contrary, he drew them close and gradually gave them access to his household. His intention was undoubtedly good: henceforth they would mend their ways, and he would turn their hearts to good. In particular, they really were men of war from their youth and magnates of wealth. Avot deRabbi Natan, chapter 5, says that the Sadducees used silver and gold vessels. Yochanan had himself been a warrior from his youth and fought many wars against all the peoples neighboring Judea. This party undoubtedly displayed its prowess in battle and presented itself in a favorable light. Yochanan rejoiced at this, for peace had been made within the country.

How aptly our sages spoke figuratively in Shabbat 56b: “When Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter, Gabriel descended and planted a reed in the sea; a sandbank rose around it, and upon it a great city was built.” This brought about the nation’s destruction. Had Solomon looked with an open eye, he would have seen that this was in truth the first cause of the destruction, for through it the kingdom was taken from him, divided and shattered into fragments. Likewise, had Yochanan seen that the first step he took for the benefit of the Sadducees was the first step toward the king of terrors and the nation’s destruction, he would not have acted thus. Without noticing, he was swept along by the current of the times after the ways of the Sadducees. For when he conquered the people of Edom, he compelled them to circumcise their flesh. Had he consulted the Sanhedrin and the sages of the Torah, he would not have done so, for “converts are as troublesome to Israel as a skin disease.” Indeed, from them came that shoot of arrogance, the wicked tyrant Herod, who killed the entire family of the Maccabees and brought about the people’s destruction. But Yochanan listened to the advice of the Sadducees and acted at their bidding, so that all the inhabitants of the country should be under one religion, although he knew well that even afterward they remained complete gentiles in every detail of religion. Evidence for this is that his son Aristobulus, who was a thoroughgoing Sadducee, likewise compelled the people of Itur to circumcise their foreskins when he conquered them. He did not do so because he feared God, but, as we have said, because this was the Sadducees’ way: when the Greeks held the upper hand, they wanted all the people to assimilate among the Greeks and become one people; when Israel’s sun rose, they wanted all the conquered peoples to be, at least outwardly, under Israel’s religion.[^4]

Although Yochanan himself was faithful to his religion and his people, his sons, who were constantly in the company of the Sadducean grandees, had been brought up at their knees from their youth. Over the course of decades, the Sadducees saw that they had driven a peg into a secure place, for half the nation had already been placed in their hands.

But the heads of the Sanhedrin in his days were Yehoshua ben Perachya, the lion of the company, and Nittai the Arbelite. All the people clung to them with self-sacrificing devotion; the prince of the Jews was a righteous man, and Torah and the fear of God grew among the people. Thus the Sadducees gnashed their teeth but could accomplish nothing. Would these vipers be content with the half that had been given them? They wished to turn everything upside down. But how could such a thing be done without the prince—the high priest? Therefore, patiently and in secret, they plotted to find an accusation against those who upheld the Torah: that their hearts were not whole with the prince’s household. They sought to sever the thread of love binding Yochanan to the Pharisees. “If you have labored and found, believe it”: complaints were already being heard among the living that the prince’s household did not behave properly and that their hearts were divided from those who upheld the Torah. A rumor was also heard among the people that Yochanan himself was unfit to be high priest and personally perform the service, because his mother had been taken captive at Modi'im, and by rabbinic law a captive woman is disqualified from the priesthood.[^5]

It is very plausible that the Sadducees themselves spread this rumor, until even some individual Pharisees believed it. From these spiders’ webs they wove a strong, stout rope with which to draw Yochanan into their company and sever the thread of blue binding him to the Pharisees.

One of the Sadducean leaders, named Eleazar ben Po'irah (called Yonatan in Antiquities), was a scoffer, evil-hearted and worthless. He was a faithful friend of Yochanan the High Priest. This is itself sure evidence that Yochanan had already fallen from his holiness: that a man of such corrupt character should be a faithful friend of the prince. With his smooth tongue, he continually spoke to Yochanan’s heart, saying he heard that the sages of Israel were not wholeheartedly loyal to him. Yochanan paid no heed, but this worthless fellow found an opportunity to show the prince that he was speaking the truth.

This is what is related in Kiddushin 66a. Abaye said: It was taught that an incident occurred with King Yannai. (Abaye follows his own view in Berakhot 29a, “Yannai and Yochanan are one and the same”; in Antiquities, however, the story is told of Yochanan Hyrcanus, agreeing with Rava’s view there.) He went to Kovalit in the wilderness and conquered sixty towns there. On his return he rejoiced greatly and summoned all the sages of Israel—“They brought mallow onto tables of gold, and ate.” (Antiquities relates at length that he asked the sages, “Am I transgressing anything in the Torah or any rabbinic rule? Tell me, and I will mend my ways.” They replied, “No, our lord.”) But Eleazar ben Po'irah the scoffer said to him, “The hearts of the Pharisees are against you.” “What shall I do to them?” He said, “Stand before them wearing the high priest’s frontlet between your eyes”—then they would speak the truth. And so it was: an elder was there, named Yehudah ben Gedidyah, who said to him, “King Yannai, the crown of kingship is enough for you. Leave the crown of priesthood to Aaron’s descendants.” For they said that his mother had been taken captive at Modi'im.[^6]

As we said above, it is plausible that the Sadducees themselves spread this false rumor. Thus, when Yochanan began to investigate and inquire into the matter, it was not substantiated, and the sages of Israel separated in anger. Antiquities relates that the sages of Israel were angry with the Pharisee Yehudah ben Gedidyah for uttering a falsehood. But the villain Eleazar would neither rest nor be still. He said to Yochanan, “Do you imagine they are truly angry with the man who slandered you? They too believe it; they merely fear you. Make a test: ask the Pharisaic sages to impose a punishment on the slanderer.” He did so, and the sages of Israel ruled in accordance with the explicit law that one who brings an evil report is flogged. Then the worthless fellow found a shield with which to fortify his position, and said to Yochanan, “That is the law for an ordinary Israelite; and for you, a king and high priest, is that to be the law as well?” “What shall I do?” “If you listen to my advice, trample them.” “And what will become of the Torah?” “It is rolled up and lying in a corner. Whoever wishes to learn may come and learn.” Immediately the evil burst forth, and all the sages of Israel were killed. The world lay desolate until Shimon ben Shetach came and restored the Torah to its former state. Our sages tell only the outcome in the briefest form; Antiquities relates it at greater length, and in fact the affair lasted several years. Other passages in the words of our sages contain incidents that belong here. At that time Yochanan separated from the Pharisees and established a Sanhedrin of Sadducees, while the Pharisees scattered in every direction. Yehoshua ben Perachya then fled to Alexandria in Egypt and remained there until Yochanan’s son Yannai became king. Shimon ben Shetach, the king’s brother-in-law, acted wisely and gradually pushed the Sadducees out of the Sanhedrin. He then summoned Yehoshua ben Perachya to Jerusalem, as explained in his entry.

The scholar Derenbourg, in his valuable book Massa Eretz Yisrael, page 22, says concerning the Sanhedrin: “But from all the different accounts in the books of the Talmud, which contradict one another”—he does not cite a single place where they contradict one another—he says that Yochanan the High Priest founded a Sanhedrin whose heads were Yehoshua ben Perachya and Nittai the Arbelite: “But what surprises us is why he chose two men from the party of the Pharisees, from whom he had already withdrawn when he founded the Sanhedrin and became their adversary.” Thus far his words. With due respect, he made a great mistake. On the contrary: it was then that Yehoshua ben Perachya fled, and Shimon then founded a Sanhedrin of Sadducees.[^7]

He likewise says there, on page 46, note a, that Yochanan Hyrcanus was president of the Hasmonean court. With due respect, he has confused an entirely different matter. Although Yochanan was great in Torah and served as high priest, he was never president of the Sanhedrin. In Avot, which discusses those who received the Torah one from another and names the president and the head of court, the name of Yochanan the High Priest is not found. The Hasmonean court is an entirely different matter. This concerns the time when Yehudah the Maccabee and his brothers were far from Jerusalem, in the town of Mikhmas; they undoubtedly established a court within their camp.[^8] Of its enactments there remains the decree concerning gentile women, as explained in their entries.[^9] But what has this to do with the days of Yochanan the High Priest, when the Hasmonean court had already ceased to exist? The Sanhedrin in his days enjoyed abundant peace, with Yehoshua ben Perachya at its head, until Yochanan became a Sadducee and decreed that anyone who observed the Pharisees’ practices should be punished. The Pharisees undoubtedly opposed him with all their strength, and the quarrel broke out until he wrought great slaughter among them.

But anyone who says that he abolished the Oral Torah is simply mistaken. If so, he would have had to abolish the commandment of peri'ah, which is not explicit in the Torah, and likewise the commandment of tefillin and the like. At the very least, he would have had to gather great sages to interpret the Torah according to his new approach, and also to observe Shavuot after the Sabbath. Had so great a thing happened, all the people would have laid down their lives over it, and our sages would not have been silent. The truth, however, is that, Heaven forbid, he did not touch anything in the Oral Torah; he abolished only rabbinic enactments. Consequently the law concerning a captive woman was annulled, and there was neither a prohibition nor a slur; this is clear.[^10] In Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 5:10, when all Yochanan the High Priest’s enactments are enumerated, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says of them that some things he did by force: his abolition of the tithe declaration was blameworthy, for after Eleazar ben Petirah and Yehudah ben Peturah came, they took them by force. This Eleazar is undoubtedly the villain Eleazar ben Po'irah mentioned in Kiddushin 66a. Were it not for their statement there that his abolition of the “awakeners” was praiseworthy—and likewise the Bavli at the end of Sotah, where the meaning is explained as those who said, “Awake! Why do You sleep?”—one might say that this too was blameworthy. For when he became a Sadducee he abolished all the rabbinic enactments, especially the captive-woman law, which affected him and his reputation. That would be the meaning of their saying he abolished the “awakeners”: those who raised the accusation against him that he was the son of a captive woman. Once he abolished the rabbinic enactments, the people raising the accusation against him were silenced.[^11]

Our sages spared his honor. Since he had been good to Israel throughout his life, his enactments remained in the Mishnah in his name, for praise and glory. According to the testimony of Antiquities, he reigned thirty years and commanded that his wife rule after him. But his son Aristobulus did not listen to him: he starved his mother to death and placed the royal crown on his own head. Yet he died in the prime of life, for he reigned only one year. His wife Shlominyon, the sister of Shimon ben Shetach, married his brother Yannai, as explained in his entry.

notes.text: The Books of the Hasmoneans is the source’s title for the Maccabean books. Dakh and Modi’it retain the forms used here; elsewhere in the entry the place is called Modi’im.

Dorot HaRishonim is abbreviated דו״הר. Hyman’s proposal distinguishes a ruling high priest from the priest performing the Temple service and takes the eighty years collectively, rather than as Yochanan’s individual tenure. Yosifin retains the source’s יוסיפין; Massa Eretz Yisrael is the work he later names as Derenbourg’s.

Demai is produce whose tithing is uncertain. “Awakeners” and “strikers” translate המעוררים and הנוקפים. “He removed the tithe” follows the wording here; the later discussion specifies the tithe declaration. The locators Ma’aser Sheni 5:15 and Sotah 9:10 are Hyman’s.
“The king of terrors” is a biblical image for death. The source calls the other conquered people בני יטור, rendered “the people of Itur.”

The allegation concerns Yochanan’s priestly descent: his mother’s supposed captivity would disqualify him from priestly service. “If you have labored and found, believe it” is used ironically of the plotters’ success.

The tzitz, here “frontlet,” is the high priest’s inscribed gold plate. The source names the elder יהודה בן גדידיה, rendered Yehudah ben Gedidyah. Its wording “mallow” refers to the food on the gold tables.

The source reads “Shimon then founded a Sanhedrin of Sadducees.” This conflicts with its nearby account, which assigns the Sadducean Sanhedrin to Yochanan and the restoration to Shimon ben Shetach. Hyman’s interruption about contradictory Talmudic accounts is set off from his quotation of Derenbourg.
After Mikhmas the source has או בל״ס, literally “or, without doubt”; the connection of “or” is unclear. Hyman nevertheless says that they established a court in their camp.
נשו״ג is an abbreviated reference to gentile women. Hyman does not set out the decree’s detailed terms here.

Peri’ah is the uncovering of the glans during circumcision. Hyman distinguishes the Oral Torah itself from rabbinic enactments and argues that abolishing the latter would remove the captive-woman restriction invoked against Yochanan.

Hyman identifies Eleazar ben Petirah with Eleazar ben Po’irah; Yehudah ben Peturah is named separately. “They took them by force” has an unspecified object in this sentence. His alternative reading of “awakeners” depends on the sense of עורר as raising an objection or accusation; he explicitly acknowledges the competing, favorable interpretation of the Temple practice.
